acid-strength-structure-s1.title: Acetic acid and three substituted versions
acid-strength-structure-s1.text: Each acid loses the H on its –COOH group. In the substituted acids, one or two H atoms on the CH₃ carbon are replaced by halogen atoms.

acid-strength-structure-s2.title: Oxyacids of chlorine and the halogens
acid-strength-structure-s2.text: In every acid below the acidic H is bonded to an O atom, and that O is bonded to the central atom (H–O–X). Electronegativity values are on the Pauling scale.

table.caption: Structure, electronegativity of the central atom, and Ka at 25 °C

acid-strength-structure-s3.title: Three organic molecules
acid-strength-structure-s3.html:
Ethanol, CH₃CH₂–O–H: Ka ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁶.

Acetic acid, CH₃–C(=O)–O–H: Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵.

Methylamine, CH₃–NH₂ (N has one lone pair): Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴.

items.q: Why is chloroacetic acid a stronger acid than acetic acid?
options: Electronegative Cl draws electron density away and stabilizes the conjugate base
The Cl atom gives the molecule a second acidic hydrogen atom that can ionize too
Chloroacetic acid has a larger molar mass, so its O–H bond is longer
The Cl atom makes the C=O bond into a single bond, which releases the proton

why.correct: An electron-withdrawing Cl two carbons away draws electron density from the –COO⁻ group, so the negative charge of ClCH₂COO⁻ is less concentrated and the ion is more stable. A more stable conjugate base means a larger Ka.
options: Right: electron withdrawal stabilizes the conjugate base.
The acidic H is still the one on –COOH; Cl replaces a C–H hydrogen, which is not acidic.
Molar mass does not set acid strength; the effect comes from electronegativity.
The C=O bond is still there; Cl changes electron density, not the bonding pattern.

items.q: Fluoroacetic acid has a larger Ka than chloroacetic acid. What does this show?
options: A more electronegative substituent gives a stronger acid
A larger halogen atom in the same position gives a stronger acid
The H–F bond in fluoroacetic acid ionizes
Fluorine adds extra resonance structures to the conjugate base

why.correct: F (electronegativity 4.0) pulls harder than Cl (3.2), so FCH₂COO⁻ is more stabilized and FCH₂COOH ionizes more.
options: Right: the stronger the pull, the more stable the anion.
F is smaller than Cl, yet its acid is stronger, so size is not the cause here.
There is no H–F bond: F is bonded to carbon, and the acidic H is on –COOH.
F does not create new resonance forms of the carboxylate; its effect is a pull through the bonds.

items.q: What is the pH of 0.10 M chloroacetic acid? (Check the small-x assumption.)

mistakes.why: Value: the small-x shortcut gives x as 12% of 0.10, over the 5% limit. Solve x² + Ka·x − Ka·C = 0.
Value: chloroacetic acid is stronger than acetic acid but still weak (Ka ≪ 1); it does not ionize fully.

items.q: Trichloroacetic acid, Cl₃CCOOH, is not in the table. Which Ka is most consistent with the trend?

why.correct: Each Cl added pulls more electron density from the carboxylate, so Ka rises with every substitution: 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ → 1.4 × 10⁻³ → 5.5 × 10⁻² → larger still for three.
options: Right: three Cl atoms, the largest Ka of the series.
That is the value for two Cl atoms; a third Cl should increase it.
That is the value for one Cl atom.
This would make it weaker than acetic acid, against the trend.

items.q: Which conjugate base is the strongest base? Select one.
options: CH₃COO⁻
ClCH₂COO⁻
Cl₂CHCOO⁻
FCH₂COO⁻

why.correct: Kb = Kw/Ka, so the weakest acid (acetic acid, smallest Ka) has the strongest conjugate base. Its negative charge is the least stabilized, so it holds a proton most readily.
options: Right: smallest Ka, largest Kb.
Chloroacetate is stabilized by the Cl, so it is a weaker base than acetate.
With two Cl atoms its charge is the most spread out: the weakest base here.
Fluoroacetate is stabilized even more than chloroacetate.

items.q: Which two acids in the table isolate the effect of the central atom's electronegativity?
options: HOCl and HOBr
HOCl and HOClO
HOClO and HOI
HOBr and HOClO

why.correct: HOCl and HOBr have the same structure (H–O–X, no extra O), so the only difference is the central atom.
options: Right: same structure, different central atom.
These share the central atom; they isolate the number of O atoms.
These differ in both the central atom and the number of O atoms.
These differ in both the central atom and the number of O atoms.

items.q: Why is HOClO a much stronger acid than HOCl?
options: In ClO₂⁻ the negative charge is spread over two O atoms
HOClO has two acidic hydrogen atoms that can both ionize
The extra O atom makes the O–H bond shorter and stronger
Cl has a higher electronegativity in HOClO than in HOCl

why.correct: In ClO₂⁻ the negative charge is shared between two O atoms (two resonance forms), and the extra O pulls electron density from the O–H bond. Both make the conjugate base more stable and the acid stronger.
options: Right: more O, a more stable conjugate base.
HOClO has one H, bonded to O; it is monoprotic.
The extra O weakens the O–H bond by pulling electron density away from it.
Electronegativity is a property of the element; Cl is the same atom in both.

items.q: Based on the table, how does acid strength change from HOCl to HOBr to HOI, and why?
options: It decreases, because a less electronegative central atom pulls less electron density from the O–H bond
It increases, because larger atoms hold the H more weakly
It decreases, because the O–H bond gets shorter
It stays the same, because each acid has one O atom

why.correct: Ka falls from 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ to 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ to 2.3 × 10⁻¹¹ as the central atom's electronegativity falls from 3.2 to 2.7. A weaker pull leaves more electron density in the O–H bond and on the O of the anion, so the anion is less stable.
options: Right: the Ka data match the electronegativity order.
In oxyacids the H is on O, not on the halogen, so the halogen's size is not the deciding factor; the data show the acids getting weaker.
The O–H bond length barely changes; the trend follows electronegativity.
The Ka values span three powers of ten, so strength is not the same.

items.q: What is the pH of 0.20 M NaOBr?

mistakes.why: Value: OBr⁻ is a base. Use Kb = Kw/Ka of HOBr to find [OH⁻].
Value: that is the pOH; subtract from 14.00.

items.q: Both ethanol and acetic acid have an O–H group. Why is acetic acid about 10¹¹ times stronger?
options: Resonance spreads the charge of acetate over two O atoms
Acetic acid has more hydrogen atoms
Ethanol is a liquid at room temperature, so its O–H bond holds
Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water and acetic acid does not

why.correct: CH₃COO⁻ has two equivalent resonance structures, each O carrying the charge half the time. CH₃CH₂O⁻ has no such spreading, so it is far less stable and ethanol barely ionizes.
options: Right: resonance delocalizes the charge of the carboxylate.
Only one H, on the –COOH group, is acidic; the C–H hydrogens are not.
Acetic acid is also a liquid at room temperature; the state is not the cause.
Both molecules hydrogen-bond with water.

items.q: When methylamine acts as a base in water, which atom accepts the proton?
options: The N atom, using its lone pair
The C atom, which has four bonds
An H atom on the N
The C atom, using a lone pair

why.correct: A Brønsted-Lowry base needs a lone pair to bond to H⁺. The N lone pair forms the new N–H bond: CH₃NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻.
options: Right: the nitrogen lone pair.
Carbon has four bonds and no lone pair, so it cannot accept a proton here.
An H atom cannot accept another proton; the new bond forms to N.
The carbon in methylamine has no lone pair.

items.q: What is the pH of 0.050 M methylamine?

mistakes.why: Value: the small-x estimate is 9% of 0.050, over 5%. Solve the quadratic for [OH⁻].
Value: that is the pOH; subtract from 14.00.

items.q: A molecule has both a –COOH group and an –NH₂ group. In a strongly acidic solution, where is the extra proton most likely to be found?
options: On the N of the –NH₂ group, giving –NH₃⁺
On the C=O carbon of the –COOH group
On a C–H carbon
On the O–H oxygen, which then loses water

why.correct: The amine N has a lone pair and is the basic site, so in strong acid it becomes –NH₃⁺. The –COOH group stays un-ionized.
options: Right: the amine nitrogen is the basic site.
A carbon with four bonds has no lone pair to accept H⁺.
Carbon atoms with C–H bonds have no lone pairs.
The –COOH oxygen is not the basic site here; the amine N, with its lone pair, is a far stronger base and takes the proton.

items.q: Rank these acids from weakest to strongest: H₂O, H₂S, H₂Se. (Bond enthalpies: O–H 463, S–H 363, Se–H 276 kJ/mol.)
options: H₂O
H₂S
H₂Se

why.correct: Down a group, the central atom gets larger, the bond to H gets longer and weaker, and the negative charge of the anion is spread over a larger volume. So H₂Se gives up H⁺ most readily. (Here bond strength wins over electronegativity, which falls down the group.)

items.q: HCl, HBr and HI are all strong in water, but HF is weak. Which factor best explains why HF holds its proton?
options: The H–F bond is short and strong, and F⁻ is small
F is the least electronegative halogen
HF molecules are nonpolar
F⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so it holds H⁺

why.correct: F is a small atom, so the H–F bond is short and strong (567 kJ/mol), and F⁻ holds its charge in a tiny volume. Both oppose giving up H⁺, so HF is the one weak hydrohalic acid.
options: Right: bond strength and the small anion.
F is the most electronegative element.
H–F is very polar; polarity alone would suggest a strong acid, which is why bond strength matters here.
F⁻ is the conjugate base of a weak acid; that is the point to explain.

items.q: Across period 2, the acidity of CH₄, NH₃, H₂O and HF increases. Which property explains this trend?
options: The electronegativity of the atom bonded to H
The number of H atoms in each molecule
The size of the central atom
The molar mass of each compound

why.correct: Across a period the atoms are similar in size, so electronegativity wins: a more electronegative atom makes the X–H bond more polar and holds the negative charge of X⁻ more easily.
options: Right: electronegativity rises from C to F.
Fewer H atoms do not cause a stronger acid; this is a coincidence of these formulas.
Across a period, atoms get slightly smaller, not larger.
Molar mass barely changes and is not the cause.

items.q: Which changes make an acid HA stronger? Select all that apply.
options: Adding resonance structures that spread the charge of A⁻
Placing an electronegative atom near the acidic H
Replacing the O–H with a C–H at the same position
Making the conjugate base less stable

why.correct: Anything that stabilizes A⁻ (spreading its charge by resonance or pulling electron density with an electronegative atom) shifts HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ to the right.
options: Right: delocalized charge, a more stable anion.
Right: electron withdrawal stabilizes A⁻.
C is less electronegative than O; C–H bonds are far less acidic.
A less stable conjugate base means a weaker acid.
